description: Direct vision of the Lord: most knowers see him within their own body; only gods, a hundred sages, a hundred kings, a hundred gandharvas and the like see him as all-pervading. The gods' liberation comes when Hari becomes directly perceived to them.
The Turīya form of Viṣṇu at the dvādaśānta, not seen in ordinary life, is sometimes seen by the fully concentrated who have reached the sixteenth kalā and have direct vision.
When the worshipper sits with the body straight, the suṣumnā shines, lit above the crown by the sun's rays, and in the heart-lotus Nārāyaṇa is contemplated.
notes: Stated as part of the contemplation in worship, not as a spontaneous sign.

description: In deep sleep the soul, covered by tamas, rests in Hari as Prājña, neither desiring nor seeing; yet the witness perceives time even then.
Dreams are real, produced from latent impressions by the Lord as Taijasa within the mind.
At the knower's death the tip of the heart lights up, illumining the door by which he departs through the crown.

The liberated abide in various worlds up to the Milk Ocean, in sālokya, sārūpya, sāmīpya or sāyujya; those in sāyujya enter the Lord and come out; each class enjoys a hundredfold more bliss than the one below.

The tradition's account of Madhva's feats as Vāyu's avatāra: eating a thousand plantains to meet a king's test, his toenail shining to give light, setting a huge rock in place, crossing the Gaṅgā without a boat, subduing a Yavana king with words, carrying the Kṛṣṇa image thirty youths could not lift.
notes: The tradition presents these as signs of his identity; no text checked here comments on powers as obstacles.

description: Devotees hold that Rāghavendra, who entered his brindāvana alive, remains present at Mantrālaya and answers prayers.
notes: Living devotional belief; no textual source checked.
